newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels stand firm on freedom for comrades.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels stand firm on freedom for comrades.

text.p: Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages, unbowed by the resolve of Peruvian and Japanese leaders not to yield to their demands, vowed again on Saturday to release the captives only after jailed guerrillas are freed.

"Until now the hypothesis that has been mentioned (by the government) is a peaceful solution but one without concession," rebel leader Nestor Cerpa told the CBS Telenoticias network. "That signifies that it is the MRTA that has to concede. That will never happen. We will not step back.

"So whatever option that the government takes, let it take it once and for all, whatever it is," Cerpa added in the interview. "We have no problem. We have come for one goal and we will not renounce it."

The roughly 15 armed rebels of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) have conditioned the release of their hostages, held in the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima for 46 days, on the freedom of about 400 jailed guerrillas.

Cerpa's comments came after Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori, in an emergency summit in Toronto, pledged not to yield to the demands of the rebels but agreed to push for talks with them.
"There will be absolutely no release of MRTA prisoners," Fujimori told a news conference after the two-hour closed meeting, rejecting the rebels' key demand.
"We received today a great backing from the Japanese government for our strategy to search for a peaceful solution to this incident," he said.

Most of the hostages have been released, but the rebels have kept those they consider the most important bargaining chips including Fujimori's brother, two Peruvian cabinet ministers and about 25 Japanese businessmen and diplomats.

A Japanese official told Reuters after the meeting that "the biggest achievement of the summit was the agreement to promote the opening of preliminary dialogue between the Peruvian government and the MRTA group."
MRTA international spokesman Isaac Velazco said in an interview from Hamburg that the Peruvian government must now take the next step with a proposal for talks.
"The ball is in their court," he told Reuters. "The only peaceful solution is with a serious proposal for negotiations that contemplate the freedom for the prisoners."
Hashimoto has been uneasy about Peru's hawkish line with the MRTA rebels and specifically with aggressive actions by Peruvian police outside the compound.
Fujimori told the news conference that Peruvian police would not continue their campaign of provoking the rebels.
In Lima on Saturday, police for the first time in days refrained from blasting martial music from speakers at the diplomatic compound in the middle of the night.
Police have played the music and paraded convoys of armoured personnel carriers outside the residence to erode the resistence of the rebels.
